title: Emotional Engineering for AI-Oriented Infrastructure Operators
subtitle: Trust, agency and ethical adoption in systems that act
blurb: The book expands the commissioned emotions document into a broader guide for AI-infrastructure operators. It treats AFGR as an operator heuristic, not a validated universal psychological sequence. Research, proposed practices, illustrative examples and STPI operating observations are distinguished. No invented author biography, endorsements, customer outcomes or interviews are claimed.

title: The Tight Bucket
subtitle: Designing constraint-native digital businesses
case_disclosure: TightBucket was commissioned by the same owner who commissions the work of Jacaranda Labs Think Tank. It is a bounded case, not an independent evaluation.
blurb: The book uses TightBucket, a website "revenue-leak" auditing service built in three days in October 2026 by its owner working with AI coding agents, as a running case. TightBucket had not launched commercially at the time of writing: it had taken no payments, so the book reports design, governance and measured operating data, not commercial results. TightBucket was commissioned by the same owner who commissions the work of Jacaranda Labs Think Tank; it is a bounded case, not an independent evaluation. Research findings, measured facts about the case, and proposed frameworks are labelled separately.

title: Constraint-Native Business Model Design
subtitle: Quota-bounded autonomy, proof-first acquisition and verification debt in a zero-cash, AI-built venture
series: Jacaranda Labs Think Tank Working Paper 2026-01
case_disclosure: TightBucket was commissioned by the same owner who commissions the work of Jacaranda Labs Think Tank. The case is not an independent evaluation.
blurb: The paper offers constraint-native business model design as a design mode, quota-bounded autonomy as a governance mechanism, a coded log of 43 review defects, and seven testable propositions. Evidence is the venture's code, documents, commit history and three days of usage telemetry checked against the cloud provider's own analytics. It is a single pre-revenue case, so its propositions are offered for testing, not as established findings.

title: Proof of Mechanism
subtitle: How leaders who build with AI agents tell a working product from a convincing demo
case_disclosure: AttestOS belongs to the same owner who commissions the work of Jacaranda Labs Think Tank. The audit and rebuild were carried out by the owner working with AI coding agents. It is a bounded case, not an independent evaluation.
blurb: The book uses AttestOS, a bot-verification service, as a candid running case. Its first version (26 October 2026) presented every conventional sign of completeness while lacking most mechanisms. An audit the next day logged 65 findings, 18 of them critical. The service was rebuilt that evening and checked again on 28 October. The book does not state how the first version was produced. It treats generation by AI as one hypothesis the evidence is consistent with. AttestOS had no customers and had taken no payments at the time of writing. The audit and rebuild were carried out by the owner working with AI coding agents: a bounded case, not an independent evaluation.

title: Simulated Completeness
subtitle: Claim–mechanism gaps, mechanism audits and the rebuild decision in an AI-era trust product
series: Jacaranda Labs Think Tank Working Paper 2026-02
case_disclosure: AttestOS belongs to the same owner who commissions the work of Jacaranda Labs Think Tank. The audit and rebuild were carried out by the owner working with AI coding agents. The case is not an independent evaluation.
blurb: The paper defines *simulated completeness* and distinguishes it from prototypes, minimum viable products, technical debt and fraud. It codes the 65 audit findings into a taxonomy of eight claim–mechanism gap types plus hygiene: 47 (72%) were gaps, including every critical and high finding. It also proposes six mechanism probes, a rebuild decision rule, an evidence contract for agent-built work and seven testable propositions. Evidence is the public commit history, the itemised audit, the production database and the service's own usage meter. It is a single pre-revenue case, so its propositions are offered for testing, not as established findings.

title: Nobody Was Watching
subtitle: How founders run autonomous growth systems without harming strangers, their brand or themselves
case_disclosure: Tapstall belongs to the same owner who commissions the work of Jacaranda Labs Think Tank. The audit and rebuild were carried out by the owner working with AI coding agents. It is a bounded case, not an independent evaluation.
blurb: The book's case is Tapstall, a shop-link service for informal merchants. On the day of its audit, its test suite passed in full while its growth pipeline was emailing non-prospects, posting into another venture's social account and running duplicate copies of itself. Each chapter sets out a question, the theory, the case, a framework, the limits of the evidence, points of debate, discussion questions and an exercise. The frameworks include the witness map, the Identity Ledger, the Clock Register, the Recipient Gate, the Stoppability Standard, armed distribution and a ninety-day programme. It is the companion to Working Paper 2026-03. The case is a single pre-revenue venture, and its frameworks are offered for testing.

title: Unwitnessed Autonomy
subtitle: Externalities, borrowed identities and duplicate clocks in an autonomous growth pipeline
series: Jacaranda Labs Think Tank Working Paper 2026-03
case_disclosure: Tapstall belongs to the same owner who commissions the work of Jacaranda Labs Think Tank. The audit and rebuild were carried out by the owner working with AI coding agents. The case is not an independent evaluation.
blurb: The paper defines *unwitnessed autonomy*: an automated system that takes consequential actions on parties outside its boundary when no party is placed to observe those effects and report them to the operator. The case is Tapstall, a shop-link service for informal and social-commerce merchants. Its test suite passed in full while the live pipeline was mailing non-prospects, sending from another venture's support mailbox, posting into another venture's social account and running duplicate copies of itself. The paper codes 24 defects (11 from the audit, 13 found during the rebuild) into nine classes. Sixteen (67%) are witness gaps, and none of the 24 was found by a test. It proposes a five-point witness map (identity, clock, effect, recipient, stop), four "one-of" rules and seven testable propositions. It is a single pre-revenue case, so its propositions are offered for testing, not as established findings.

title: The Sovereign Micro-Enterprise
subtitle: A Governance-First Architecture for Zero-Capital Agentic Businesses
series: Founding field report of the Distributed Cognitive Autonomous Infrastructure programme
case_disclosure: The case, Hunta, was the author's own business. It was retired in October 2026; the paper's operating claims describe it as it ran in September and October 2026 and are not independent validation of later systems.
blurb: The founding field report of the Distributed Cognitive Autonomous Infrastructure programme. It documents Hunta, a one-person, zero-capital sales and content business run by agents, and formalises four governance mechanisms: Guarded-Capability Governance, the Ledgered-Agent Pattern, the Zero-Capital Ladder and Effectuation-in-the-Loop. title: Flower and Bees
subtitle: The Jacaranda voice guide: how every page, product and message should feel
case_disclosure: Jacaranda Labs owns the six ventures the book uses as its worked examples (TightBucket, AttestOS, DeskOS, STPi, Tapstall and Open Practice). Every example of copy in the book is constructed; none quotes a customer or reports a result. It is an insider's manual, not an independent evaluation.
blurb: The flower does not chase the bee. It opens, it is honest about what it holds, and it is easy to find. This manual applies that idea to the words a business publishes. It separates hype, which is invented feeling, from emotion, which is real feeling named accurately. It sets out five parts every page needs (recognition, the cost, the after, the proof and the small door) and nine rules of truth, warmth and the door. Then it works through the surfaces where words are actually made: the landing page, the product card, the first-touch email, follow-up and the sales call. Part Six applies the method to each of the six Jacaranda Labs ventures, and Part Eight is the toolkit. Every example of copy in the book is constructed; none quotes a customer or reports a result.

title: The Ledger and the Shopkeeper
subtitle: Building commerce for the markets the platforms forgot
blurb: A trade book on building a merchant rail for shops the platforms skipped — written from the release log rather than the pitch deck. Part one is the gap: the forty-tab panic, and why the obvious answer is wrong. Part two is the machine: a shop in one link, a statement that can be recomputed, quotas as a design material, the first hundred prospects, and the number that could not be dialled. Part three is the rules: never hold the money, never lie in the copy, never post to your customers. Part four is the craft — what broke, in five failure classes, and the uncomfortable arithmetic that follows.

title: Intelligence, Data and Judgement
subtitle: An applied introduction to artificial intelligence, with a production case
blurb: A textbook written to be taught from. Twenty-two chapters in five parts — foundations, the material, the machine, the case, and judgement — each with learning outcomes, a worked example, graded exercises and further reading. The disciplinary spine is three widely used curricula: COMCEC's introduction to AI and its fundamental concepts, Microsoft's Fundamentals of AI Module 1, and NITI Aayog's Let's Learn AI Base Module, each attributed and mapped chapter by chapter in the appendix. Tapstall runs through the middle of the book as the worked case, including its failures.

title: Order Without Custody
subtitle: Governance-first design for merchant commerce rails in low-infrastructure economies
blurb: Small merchants already sell at scale — through chat threads, pages and a phone number painted on a wall — but they sell without a record. This paper argues that the binding constraint at that tier is not payment capability but reconciliation, and that reconcilability is an architectural property rather than a feature. Five mechanisms are formalised against artefacts a reader can inspect: the No-Custody Rail, Admission-Gated Discovery, Reserve-Ladder Scheduling, Surface-Disjoint Multi-Tenancy and the Constrained Persuasion Doctrine. The empirical section is forensic: five classes of governance failure, each stated as a signature, a detector and a design response.

title: Grounded Cadence
subtitle: Fact-bound content operations as a governance architecture
blurb: Anyone can now emit a week of social copy. Almost no one can emit it on a schedule, from a company's own facts, without inventing customers or numbers, without spending the operator's quota on a stranger, and without a silent failure looking like a green run. This paper reports a live zero-capital writing service and formalises four mechanisms with production incidents attached: fact-bound generation, value–promo cadence, capability isolation, and fail-loud operations.

title: The Governable Enterprise
subtitle: A practical guide to evidence, authority and AI operations — lessons from DeskOS
blurb: A practitioner guide to designing AI operations that can explain their evidence, limit their authority, account for resources and recover from uncertainty. DeskOS is examined as a candid, bounded case rather than a product-success claim, and the ten operating tools are given as methods a reader can adopt rather than results a reader should assume. Prepared in PDF, editable Word, EPUB, HTML and Markdown; full text is not distributed publicly.

title: From Spreadsheet Interface to Governable Autonomy
subtitle: DeskOS as a critical design-science case of evidence, agency and resource-constrained AI infrastructure
blurb: A bounded implementation study separating generated artefacts from verified intelligence — the distinction that decides whether an operator is being informed or flattered. It proposes an Evidence–Authority–Resource Contract and a prospective evaluation protocol, and reports no customer-outcome experiment, because none was run.

title: The Musk Mirror
subtitle: How one billionaire exposed the cracks in China's innovation dream
blurb: A gallery of expert predictions, set against what was actually built. The book reads as a mirror rather than a weapon: on the rocket sceptics, the communications 'experts', the business-model critics and the CEO chorus, and on what their confidence cost. Its argument is about expertise without humility, and about the difference between a claim that sounds authoritative and a number that can be checked.

title: Traffic Is the New Oil
subtitle: The African digital wealth formula
blurb: Six chapters on the only formula that has ever run the internet — traffic, ads, money — argued for a continent that supplies the eyeballs and keeps too little of the revenue. From the awakening, through the traffic layer and the ad market, to what actually enters an account while the power is out, and a zero-capital route from nothing to a first four-figure month.

title: Pinterest Goldmine
subtitle: The traffic source nobody told you about
blurb: A complete operating manual for one under-used traffic channel: the psychology of the scroll-stop, a pin factory run from Canva on a phone, the search optimisation playbook, a scheduling system that survives real-life disruption, and the money layer that turns attention into a payout.

title: The Rocket Man Reckoning
subtitle: How China mocked Elon Musk — and why they are now panicking
blurb: The arrogance of a rising superpower, the collapse of its myths, and what one company's success reveals about the future of innovation. A short book about a decade of ridicule from established voices — academic, industrial and editorial — and what happened when the engineering arrived anyway.

title: Unchained Blueprint
subtitle: What to build when every payment door is closed
blurb: Every single door was closed: the processor that does not support your country, the payouts that are unavailable in your region, the account that has been limited. This blueprint starts from the observation that these are decisions rather than accidents, and works out what a builder in that position can still put in place.

title: The Mechanism Audit
subtitle: Evidence-first review for products that act without an operator
series: Jacaranda Labs Think Tank Working Paper 2026-04
case_disclosure: The estate audited in this paper is owned by the author. Incidents are self-reported and drawn from seven ventures operated by the same owner; no independent replication is claimed.
blurb: Software reviews were built on the assumption that a human performed every action and a second human watched. Products that commit, publish and invoice on their own have removed the witness, and the instruments of review — the demo, the screenshot, the QA script — cannot certify a mechanism nobody saw run. This paper sets out a method for auditing that class of product: a claim ledger, a mechanism map, an evidence trail, a detector and a response, with the requirement that a stranger can re-run all five. Six failure signatures are formalised — the green run, the allowlist, the credential that authenticates, the retry that published twice, the fallback that looked like output, the origin that had not propagated — each with a production incident attached from one week of operating seven ventures, and each mapped to one of six gap classes: claim–evidence, scope, capability, ownership, propagation, attribution.

title: The Mechanism Auditor
subtitle: How to review a product that runs without you
case_disclosure: The failures described are the author's own, in an estate of seven ventures he owns. They are disclosed as incidents, not as third-party case studies.
blurb: A trade book for the person who is now the only witness to software that acts on its own. Part one is the loss: the demo was a promise, and a green tick says less than everyone believes. Part two is the instrument: the claim ledger, the mechanism map, the evidence trail, the detector and the response, each with the failure it is built to catch. Part three is the field guide — six signatures, from the green run to the origin that had not yet propagated, taken from one week of ordinary operation across seven products. Part four is the practice, including a first week in the order it happened. Part five is the business of auditing: what to charge, what to refuse. Part six is the twelve rules and the uncomfortable arithmetic that follows from them.

title: The Point of Failure
subtitle: An operating manual for the person running the estate
case_disclosure: The incidents, hours and thresholds described are the author's own, in an estate of seven ventures he operates alone. Nothing here is clinical evidence and nothing here is a substitute for care from a professional.
blurb: Every component in a one-person estate has a failover — the rails retry, the bank refills, the deploys verify, the front doors are watched hourly. There is exactly one part with no redundancy, and it is not the server. This book gives the operator the treatment every other component gets: written down, checked, given limits, monitored. Five parts — the single point of failure; nine non-negotiables with the mechanism each one protects and the check that takes seconds; the bad day and the pause switch; the difference between the ledger and the self; and where a book has to stop and a person has to start. It is not therapy and says so on the first page. It is the set of structural rules that stop this specific way of working — unbounded surface, one decider, a machine that runs at 3am — from eating the person doing it.

title: Operatorship
subtitle: What ate technopreneurship, and what replaced it
case_disclosure: The specimen estate is the author's own: seven ventures, twenty-two works, five publishing rails, roughly three hours twenty minutes a week of human attention. One estate is a case, not a study, and the book says so in the chapter it reports the numbers in.
blurb: Technopreneurship was never a theory of value. It was a description of an arbitrage: capability, distribution and coordination were all scarce, and the person who had learned them held a moat priced in years. Superintelligence — capability at expert breadth, rented by the token — repriced all three at once, and what became scarce was everything that used to be free because a human was carrying it implicitly: trust, attention, taste, and the willingness to be answerable. This book does the autopsy in five parts — the word, the breakfast, the name, the curriculum and the risk — then names the successor and defines it in one sentence: operatorship is the practice of owning the consequences of machine work you did not perform. It ends with a replacement syllabus and an exam question that cannot be answered by a generated document, because its subject is a thing that either runs or does not.
